fields.v: Martin, A., Schwander, S. (2026). A Lean and Spec-Driven AI-Assisted Software Development Lifecycle for Applied AI Education: The AI-SDLC Approach. arXiv:2609.24348v1 [cs.SE], 21 Sep 2026
Preprint — arXiv:2609.24348v1 [cs.SE]; Springer LNCS-style layout, venue not stated
FHNW University of Applied Sciences and Arts Northwestern Switzerland, School of Business, Olten

Proposes an approach; secondary: Evaluates — proposes the authors' AI-SDLC lifecycle (six phases, AGENTS.md, SKILL.md files, specs) and explores it with a post-course student survey (n=13; descriptive, exploratory)
AI-SDLC (AI-Assisted Software Development Life Cycle), authors' own; evaluated version 1.0.0-beta (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.22724343); current template v1.0.0 (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.22833065)

Compact AGENTS.md (workflow rules, guardrails); phase-specific SKILL.md files (skills/ai-sdlc-*); docs/PROJECT.md (system, stack, architecture, dependencies); use case specifications under docs/specs/ (behaviour, scope, acceptance criteria, NFRs, intended tests); docs/TASKS.md (lifecycle state, tasks); optional ADRs; tests (integration, unit, E2E)

Bootstrap (project context, environment, architectural baseline) -> Specify (user story to use case spec; no implementation) -> Design (map to Clean Architecture, ADRs, tasks) -> Develop (TDD: integration -> unit -> code, Red-Green-Refactor) -> Validate (unit, integration, E2E tests, CI, release build) -> Deploy; feedback loops back on failing validation or new requirements (iterative)

No mandatory approval after each action; agent autonomous within a phase once started; human control through inspectable/modifiable persistent artefacts (specs, ADRs, tasks, tests, validation results) between phases; PR review used by some students
Full workflow (six phases) in student semester projects; adherence partial (Bootstrap, Specify, Validate most often shortened; no phase skipped)
Not stated (one use case spec per user story/change kept in docs/specs/; closest to spec-first/spec-anchored, not classified by the authors)
New projects: business-oriented software use cases developed by student teams in a semester project
Not stated (project size not given); 34 students invited, 13 complete responses
Business-oriented software (education context, BSc Business Artificial Intelligence)

Bachelor students (Business AI), student teams; median age 25 (23-32); 5 beginners, 7 basic programming knowledge, median 3 years programming; prior work mainly hobby/open source (10 of 13); high AI coding tool experience (7 daily/intensive)
None measured. Perceived: all 13 agreed they made faster progress; 4 agreed the process felt like unnecessary overhead in some phases (small tasks); survey time ~22 min (not a cost metric)
None measured objectively. Perceived: 10 of 13 agreed quality of result improved; confidence in code correctness mostly with reservations
None measured
None measured (perceived overhead and comprehension items only)

Survey: agreement items on process support, artefacts, self-instruction files, human verification, learning/productivity; adherence and perceived usefulness per phase (means 3.77-4.42 of 5); Net Promoter item (7-10, median 8); thematic coding of open answers
Manual: cross-sectional online survey (German), 5-point agreement scale with reverse-worded items; descriptive frequencies only; open answers coded thematically by one author

(1) AI-SDLC v1.0.0-beta + coding agent not stated + model not stated (student projects, survey n=13). Criterion: student perceptions (no objective criterion). Values: Specify sharpened requirements 13/13 agree (11 strongly); structured collaboration 12/13; phases gave orientation 12/13; improved quality 10/13; faster progress 13/13; would reuse 12/13; overhead in some phases 4/13; adopted code without understanding 6/13 (closed item), 11/13 (free text); following the code lowest-rated positive item; PR review ~half; NPS median 8. Quality verdict: partly (perceived positive, verification weak, self-report only). Cost verdict: partly (perceived faster, overhead for small tasks; not measured)

No comparison: single cohort, one point in time, no control group or baseline; respondents asked to compare with their 'usual way of working'. Projects not described; agents/models not controlled or reported; no acceptance tests; no repetitions; human intervention unrestricted (students drive the process)
N/A (no comparison); perceived improvement over usual way of working (10 of 13)

N/A. Authors state the design is descriptive and exploratory, not able to establish causal effects; closed ratings and free-text answers disagree in places (e.g. adopting code without understanding 6 vs 11; PR review 7 agree vs 1 mention)

Inexperienced cohort with no own process to compare (assessment may be favourable); 13 respondents from one cohort, not generalisable; results are perceived, not observed behaviour. Open issues: confidence vs comprehension gap; repository-local instructions need maintenance (forgotten conventions, files growing too large); artefacts not updated automatically across team members' agents; ADRs rarely used; need lightweight path for small changes; add security/monitoring step. Future: repeat with later and more experienced cohorts; objective measures (code quality, coverage, adherence, review activity)

Inconsistencies: conclusion says verification relied on trying software (5 mentions) more than tests/CI (3 mentions), findings list tests/CI second without a count; conclusion reports 11 of 12 agreeing instruction files helped adhere to conventions, while findings report 11 of 13 found it clear how to use them (different items/denominators). Figure values jumbled in extraction; counts taken from text. AI-SDLC artefacts on Zenodo (both versions); questionnaire availability not stated. No pre-registration. Programming language: Not stated. Generative AI used for language editing and Python implementation (declared)

fields.why: Artefacts are light Markdown files published on Zenodo and used by bachelor students (pp. 2-4), but the paper only says 'contemporary coding agents' (p. 2) and states no agent, model, compute or token cost, so the requirements Q13 asks for are not stated. Partly is a reading; Yes if only the artefacts count, No under the 'missing information scores No' rule if the author reads it strictly.
